'''''Ceratocapnos claviculata''''', the '''climbing corydalis''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a weak scrambling plant in the family [[Papaveraceae]]. It is endemic to Europe, growing mostly near the [[Atlantic Europe|Atlantic fringe]].<ref name=BSBI>[http://species.bsbi.org.uk/html/ceratocapnos_claviculata.html Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100201140232/http://species.bsbi.org.uk/html/ceratocapnos_claviculata.html |date=February 1, 2010 }}</ref>

==Description==
This delicate looking plant is a hairless [[Annual plant|annual]] (or occasionally [[Perennial plant|perennial]]) up to a metre tall with weak, often pinkish, clambering stems. The leaves are pale to medium green, doubly compound, the leaflets being well-stalked and divided into three to five sub-leaflets, and ending in a branching tendril. It blooms between May and September in the UK.<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=36 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=9780276002175}}</ref> The flowers are small, about {{convert|6|mm|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=Readers/> pale creamy-yellow, in short [[Glossary of botanical terms#axillary|axilliary]] spikes. Each flower is elongated and tubular with a lip and spur and stamens in two bundles. The seed pods are short, usually narrowing between the two seeds.<ref>McClintock, D. and Fitter, R. ''The Pocket Guide to Wild Flowers''. Collins (1955)</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was first published as ''Ceratocapnos claviculata'' by [[Magnus Lidén]] in '[[Anales del Jardín Botánico de Madrid|Anales Jard. Bot. Madrid]]' vol.41 on page 221 in 1984, based on an earlier description by [[Carl Linnaeus]] under the name ''Fumaria claviculata''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ceratocapnos claviculata (L.) Lidén is an accepted name|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2711063|website=23 March 2012|publisher=theplantlist.org|accessdate=6 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Papaveraceae Ceratocapnos claviculata (L. ) Lidén|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=913782-1|publisher=ipni.org|accessdate=6 November 2017}}</ref>

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''claviculata'' refers to having tendrils or being tendrilled.<ref>D. Gledhill {{Google books|NJ6PyhVuecwC|The Names of Plants|page=10}}</ref>
 
==Distribution==
This species is known from several countries in western Europe, [[Belgium]], [[Denmark]], [[France]], [[Germany]], [[Ireland]], [[Netherlands]], [[Spain]], [[Portugal]] and [[Norway]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hassler|first1=M.|title=Species Details : Ceratocapnos claviculata (Samp.) Lidén|url=http://www.catalogueoflife.org/col/details/species/id/9c094b3b2fb417808055ee171d36617e|date=September 2017|accessdate=6 November 2017}}</ref> The largest proportion of the global population is found in the United Kingdom. It grows in most counties in Britain especially the more western ones, but is absent from [[Orkney]], [[Shetland]] and the [[Outer Hebrides]] and rare in [[Ireland]].<ref name=BSBI/> UK conservation status is least concern as of 2005.<ref>[http://sppaccounts.bsbi.org/content/ceratocapnos-claviculata-1.html BSBI Species Accounts - Ceratocapnos claviculata]</ref>

==Ecology==
Climbing corydalis tends to grow on the edges of woodlands and previously wooded sites. It prefers acid soils, sandy or peaty, and usually in sheltered and half shaded positions. It is sometimes abundant in disturbed parts of recently cleared plantations or woods, clambering over wood debris. It grows well in impoverished soil under [[bracken]], perhaps because it flowers early in the year before the fronds develop fully.<ref name=BSBI/>
It is the food plant for the [[weevil]], ''[[Procas granulicollis]]'' and the [[beetle]], ''[[Sirocalodes mixtus]]''.<ref>[http://www.bioinfo.org.uk/html/t1121.htm BioInfo (UK)] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724130818/http://www.bioinfo.org.uk/html/t1121.htm |date=July 24, 2011 }}</ref>
Pollination is by [[Western honey bee|honey bees]] and [[bumblebee]]s.<ref>[Perspectives in Plant Ecology, Evolution and Systematics - Biological Flora of Central Europe: Ceratocapnos claviculata]</ref>
